title: Adult plasticity and neurogenesis debates
text:
CHAPTER 11. PLASTICITY AND DEVELOPMENT
SECTION 11.2. ADULT PLASTICITY AND THE NEUROGENESIS DEBATES

Is the adult brain fixed?

For much of the twentieth century, a common view held that the adult brain is largely fixed. Cajal wrote, in a frequently quoted passage from his work on degeneration and regeneration of the nervous system (1913 to 1914), that in adult centers the nerve paths are something fixed and immutable: everything may die, nothing may be regenerated. He added that it was for the science of the future to change this harsh decree if possible. Critical period research (section 11.1) seemed to reinforce the idea that plasticity is mostly a feature of youth.

The science of the future did change the decree, at least partly. Since the 1980s, researchers have found that the adult brain retains substantial plasticity: cortical maps reorganize after injury and with training, synapses are continually formed and eliminated, and in some regions of some species, new neurons are born throughout life. At the same time, the extent of adult plasticity, and especially of adult neurogenesis in humans, has been the subject of vigorous debate. This section reviews the evidence.

Cortical map reorganization

Michael Merzenich, Jon Kaas, and colleagues performed a series of experiments in adult monkeys starting in the late 1970s and 1980s, mapping the somatosensory cortex (where the body surface is represented as in Penfield's homunculus, section 3.3) with microelectrodes. They found that:

- After the nerve supplying part of the hand (the median nerve) was cut, the region of cortex that had represented that part of the hand did not remain silent. Within weeks to months, it began to respond to touch on neighboring skin regions supplied by intact nerves.
- After amputation of a finger, the cortical territory of the missing finger was taken over by representations of adjacent fingers.
- Training monkeys to use particular fingertips intensively in a tactile task expanded the cortical representation of those fingertips.

In 1991, Tim Pons, Mortimer Mishkin, and colleagues reported much larger-scale reorganization in monkeys that had lost sensory input from an arm many years earlier (the "Silver Spring monkeys," who had been part of a controversial research program): the face representation had expanded into the deafferented arm region, over distances of more than a centimeter. This was more than anyone had expected from the spread of existing connections.

Phantom limbs

In humans, Vilayanur Ramachandran and colleagues reported in the early 1990s that some people who had lost an arm felt sensations in their phantom hand when their face was touched, sometimes with a systematic mapping from points on the face to points on the phantom hand. Since the face representation lies next to the hand representation in somatosensory cortex, this was interpreted as a perceptual consequence of cortical reorganization, consistent with the monkey findings. Ramachandran also developed "mirror therapy," in which patients view a mirror reflection of their intact limb to create the visual illusion that the missing limb is present and moving, which was reported to relieve phantom limb pain in some patients; controlled trials have shown mixed results.

The relationship between cortical reorganization and phantom pain has turned out to be complicated. Studies by Herta Flor and colleagues in the 1990s reported correlations between the amount of reorganization and phantom pain. Later work by Tamar Makin and colleagues, using fMRI, found that the cortical representation of the missing hand can persist for decades after amputation, and that phantom pain may be associated with preserved rather than lost representation. A more recent longitudinal study by Makin and colleagues followed patients before and after arm amputation and reported that the hand representation was largely stable. This shows that even well-known stories in neuroscience can be revised as methods improve.

Experience and expertise

Adult brains also change with learning and expertise:

- In 2000, Eleanor Maguire and colleagues reported that London taxi drivers, who must learn the layout of thousands of streets (a test called "The Knowledge"), had larger posterior hippocampi than control subjects, and that the size correlated with years of driving. A later longitudinal study (Katherine Woollett and Maguire, 2011) found that trainees who passed the test showed hippocampal growth over the training period, while those who failed did not, supporting a causal role of learning.
- In 2004, Bogdan Draganski, Arne May, and colleagues reported that learning to juggle over three months produced a transient increase in gray matter in visual motion areas, which decreased when practice stopped.
- Musicians show differences in auditory and motor cortex compared with non-musicians, with some differences correlating with the age at which training began.

Such MRI findings measure changes in volume or density, which could reflect changes in neurons, glia, blood vessels, or other tissue components. Their cellular basis is not fully understood, and some findings have not replicated well, so they should be interpreted with appropriate caution.

Synaptic turnover in the adult cortex

Two-photon microscopy (chapter 12) made it possible to image dendritic spines, the small protrusions that host most excitatory synapses, repeatedly over days and weeks in living animals. In 2002, Joshua Trachtenberg, Karel Svoboda, and colleagues reported that in adult mouse somatosensory cortex, a fraction of spines appear and disappear over days, while others are stable for months; changing sensory experience (such as trimming whiskers) increased turnover. In the same year, Jaime Grutzendler, Narayanan Kasthuri, and Wen-Biao Gan reported that most spines in adult mouse visual cortex were very stable. Differences between brain regions, ages, and methods explained part of the disagreement. Later studies showed that motor learning induces the formation of new spines in motor cortex, and that the survival of new spines correlates with retention of the learned skill (Tonghui Xu, Yi Zuo, and colleagues, 2009; Guang Yang, Feng Pan, and Wen-Biao Gan, 2009). So adult cortex combines a large stable scaffold with a smaller, dynamic population of synapses that is modified by learning.

Recovery after stroke

Stroke, caused by blockage or rupture of a blood vessel, kills brain tissue and is a leading cause of disability. Patients often recover partially over weeks to months, and part of this recovery involves plasticity: surviving regions take over functions, and connections are reorganized. Studies in animals and humans suggest that there is a period of heightened plasticity shortly after a stroke, a kind of reopened critical period, during which rehabilitation may be especially effective. John Krakauer, Steven Zeiler, and colleagues have discussed this idea. Rehabilitation strategies include intensive practice, constraint-induced movement therapy (developed by Edward Taub, in which the unaffected limb is restrained to force use of the affected limb), and, in research settings, brain stimulation and brain-computer interfaces (chapter 14).

Adult neurogenesis: a long controversy

The question of whether new neurons are born in the adult mammalian brain has a remarkable history.

In the early 1960s, Joseph Altman at MIT used a method called autoradiography with tritiated thymidine, a radioactive building block of DNA that is incorporated only into cells that are dividing. He reported labeled neurons in the hippocampus (dentate gyrus), olfactory bulb, and cortex of adult rats, suggesting that new neurons were being produced. Altman and Gopal Das published key papers in 1965. These findings were largely ignored or doubted for years, partly because they contradicted the prevailing dogma and partly because it was difficult to prove that the labeled cells were neurons.

In the 1980s, Fernando Nottebohm and colleagues showed that new neurons are produced in the brains of adult songbirds, in regions involved in song, and that neurogenesis varies with the seasons, when birds learn new songs. This made adult neurogenesis harder to dismiss in vertebrates generally.

In the 1990s, new methods, such as the synthetic thymidine analog bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) combined with markers for neurons, confirmed adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus and the olfactory system of rodents. Elizabeth Gould and colleagues reported neurogenesis in adult primates. In 1998, Peter Eriksson, Fred Gage, and colleagues published evidence of adult neurogenesis in the human hippocampus, using tissue from cancer patients who had been given BrdU for diagnostic purposes.

In rodents, studies by Gage, Gerd Kempermann, Henriette van Praag, and others showed that adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus is increased by running and by enriched environments, decreased by stress and aging, and may contribute to certain kinds of learning, such as discriminating between similar contexts (pattern separation). Some studies reported that antidepressant effects in mice depended on hippocampal neurogenesis (Luca Santarelli, Rene Hen, and colleagues, 2003).

In 2013, Kirsty Spalding, Jonas Frisen, and colleagues used an ingenious method to estimate neurogenesis in humans. Atmospheric nuclear bomb tests in the 1950s and early 1960s produced a spike in the level of carbon-14 in the atmosphere, which then declined after the test ban treaty of 1963. Since cells incorporate carbon from the environment when they divide and copy their DNA, the carbon-14 level in a cell's DNA reflects when it was born. By measuring carbon-14 in DNA from hippocampal neurons of people who died at various ages, they estimated that roughly 700 new neurons are added to each human hippocampus per day in adults, with a modest decline with age. Using the same approach, Frisen's group had earlier reported that the human olfactory bulb receives very few new neurons in adulthood, unlike in rodents, and later reported that new neurons are added to the human striatum.

The controversy flared again in 2018. Shawn Sorrells, Arturo Alvarez-Buylla, and colleagues published a study in Nature examining human hippocampal tissue from many individuals with markers for immature neurons. They reported that neurogenesis declined sharply in childhood and was undetectable in adults. In the same year, Maura Boldrini, Rene Hen, J. John Mann, and colleagues published a study in Cell Stem Cell reporting persistent neurogenesis in the hippocampus throughout adulthood, with thousands of immature neurons in older adults. In 2019, Elena Moreno-Jimenez, Maria Llorens-Martin, and colleagues reported in Nature Medicine abundant immature neurons in the hippocampus of healthy adults up to their tenth decade, with marked reductions in people with Alzheimer's disease, and argued that tissue processing methods (especially the time and method of fixation) strongly affect the detection of markers. Subsequent studies using single-cell RNA sequencing have produced conflicting results as well.

As of the time of writing, the extent and functional significance of adult neurogenesis in the human hippocampus remain debated. What seems clear is that neurogenesis is robust in the adult rodent dentate gyrus, that it declines with age in all species studied, and that methodological issues (tissue quality, marker specificity, and the challenge of studying humans) make the human question unusually hard. This is a good example of a scientific controversy in which careful researchers using different methods reach different conclusions, and where the honest answer is that the question is not yet settled.

Bridge to AI: plasticity, stability, and lifelong learning

The adult brain faces a balancing act: it must remain plastic enough to learn new things throughout life, but stable enough to preserve existing knowledge and skills. This is known in neuroscience and AI as the stability-plasticity dilemma, a term associated with Stephen Grossberg's work in the 1980s on adaptive resonance theory (ART), a family of neural network models designed to learn new categories without destroying old ones.

The brain's solutions, as suggested by this section, include:

- A mostly stable scaffold of connections with a small dynamic subset that changes with learning (spine turnover).
- Local, input-specific changes (LTP at specific synapses) rather than global changes.
- Adding new units in specific regions (adult neurogenesis, at least in rodents), which could provide fresh capacity for new memories without overwriting old ones.
- Reorganization that redirects unused resources to active inputs (map plasticity after amputation).
- Regulation of plasticity by neuromodulators and by the state of the animal (attention, arousal, reward).

Each of these has analogs in machine learning methods for continual learning, which we examine in the next section. For example, "progressive neural networks" (Andrei Rusu and colleagues, 2016) add new units for each new task while freezing old ones, much as neurogenesis might add capacity; methods that protect important weights while allowing others to change resemble the stable scaffold with a dynamic subset; and modular or sparse networks that use different subsets of units for different tasks resemble input-specific plasticity.

Summary

- Cajal's view that adult nerve paths are fixed has been revised; the adult brain retains significant plasticity.
- Merzenich, Kaas, and colleagues showed reorganization of somatosensory maps in adult monkeys after nerve injury, amputation, and training; Pons and colleagues found large-scale reorganization years after deafferentation.
- Phantom limb sensations were linked to cortical reorganization, but later studies found that missing-hand representations can persist, revising the story.
- Learning and expertise are associated with structural brain changes (taxi drivers, juggling), with cellular bases still uncertain.
- Two-photon imaging shows a stable majority of dendritic spines and a dynamic minority whose formation and survival track learning.
- Adult neurogenesis is well established in the rodent dentate gyrus; in humans, carbon-14 dating suggested ongoing hippocampal neurogenesis, but studies since 2018 disagree and the question remains open.
- The stability-plasticity dilemma links adult plasticity to continual learning in AI.
